design: field-experiment (immersive 360-degree video and spatial audio playback; participants recruited on site)
exposure: Four designed 360-degree soundscape samples from Peace Gardens recordings: V1 foreground human sound (talking/laughing) over pleasant background; V2 background human sound; V3 no human sound (control); V4 foreground loud signal sound over pleasant human background
behaviour_measure: Level of Willingness for social interactions (LoW-C/E/S) as stimulation level; soundscape suitability via SQE (stressful-peaceful; uneventful-eventful; unsafe-safe; unpleasant-pleasant)
key_finding: Only the foreground human sound sample significantly raised both soundscape suitability and willingness for social interaction, while the other three samples produced either high suitability/low stimulation or low suitability/high stimulation, and the preference varied by companion type and age group
effect_stats: Correlations of social willingness with companion types and age reported as negative coefficients R = -0.233 and R = -0.206 (Table 1, with two-sample t-tests); other effect sizes NR in excerpt

country: Vietnam (field data, Ho Chi Minh City); anechoic-chamber measurements in Japan
design: mixed (roadside video plus sound-level-meter observation of traffic; structured interviews; controlled anechoic-chamber horn experiment)
sample_n: 30 interviewees (10 motorcycle taxi drivers, 20 university student commuters); traffic recordings on Hoang Van Thu Street
exposure: Motorcycle horn use patterns: attention signals P1-P3 (single/double/triple presses of 0.5-0.7 s, 0.3-0.5 s intervals) and warning signals P4-P6 (press >1 s; multiple short presses ending in a continuous press); 125 cc electromechanical diaphragm horn driven in an anechoic chamber
behaviour_measure: Horn-use pattern typology (number of presses, press duration, inter-press interval) derived from rush-hour video/SLM recording and interviews; resulting sound pressure level and one-third octave spectra per pattern
measurement_method: observation (HD video plus calibrated sound level meter RION NL-28) and self-report (structured interviews)
key_finding: Culturally shaped repeated and prolonged horn-pressing behaviour raises sound pressure levels by up to 17 dB over a standard single press and shifts frequency content, so driver signalling behaviour is a main determinant of congested-street noise exceeding WHO daytime guidance
effect_stats: Up to 17 dB increase in SPL versus standard horn use; no inferential statistics reported (NR)

design: mixed (LAeq acoustic measurement plus soundwalks, sound diaries and mental maps, ISO 12913 protocol)
exposure: In-situ urban soundscape of five morphologically distinct zones in the old city and lower city (LAeq measured); natural, social/human and mechanical (traffic) sound components; morning versus afternoon variation
behaviour_measure: Reported avoidance of mechanically noisy streets; walking pleasantness and sound comfort ratings along predefined itineraries; weekly sound-perception heat maps by zone; mental maps of routes and sound
measurement_method: self-report (soundwalk questionnaire, sound diary, mental map) plus sensor (integrating sound level meter, LAeq)
key_finding: Natural and social sounds increased perceived comfort and safety whereas mechanical noise was associated with discomfort and avoidance behaviour in those streets, and sound comfort was moderately positively correlated with walking pleasantness
effect_stats: Morning: sound comfort vs visual perception rho = 0.58, p = 0.001, 95% CI [0.27; 0.80]; sound comfort vs walking pleasantness rho = 0.40, p = 0.033, 95% CI [0.05; 0.67]

country: UK (UCL-run online focus groups; participants from Turkiye, Germany, UK, Italy, Ireland, Switzerland)
design: survey (online expert focus groups with deductive thematic analysis)
sample_n: 12 experts (Turkish cohort n = 6, international cohort n = 6); pilot n = 12 excluded from analysis
exposure: Street soundscape components discussed by experts: natural sounds, traffic/mechanical noise, silence, religious and cultural soundmarks, temporal variation (morning vs night, events), street geometry and greenery
behaviour_measure: Thematically coded pedestrian behaviour: mobility and route choices, coping strategies, social interactions, and reported use of space (theme referenced by n = 10 of 12 participants)
key_finding: Experts reported that street soundscapes shape pedestrian mobility choices, coping strategies and social interaction, with silence perceived as either safe or unsafe depending on pedestrian density; direction is qualitative and no effect magnitude is given
effect_stats: NR (qualitative thematic analysis; behaviour theme referenced by 10 of 12 participants; 7 of 10 Healthy Streets metrics referenced)
